tuxedo / playground — ruby-prism → lossless CST

A tree with nowhere to put a space

Prism's AST knows the exact byte range of every if, every string, every keyword — but nothing about the whitespace, blank lines, or comments between them. A red/green tree reconstructs that missing trivia and gives three real tools something to build on: a formatter (rewrite trivia, keep structure), a linter (match structure, report at an absolute position), and RuboCop's semantic alignment (check a column against another node's column).

Green tree

Immutable, shared, offset-free. Every node only knows its own width — never its position or its parent — so identical subtrees can be reused freely and an edit far away never invalidates one sitting here.

If w=72
if w=2
Call w=6
Statements w=10
widths only — no absolute position, no parent link

Red tree

A thin, throwaway wrapper computed on navigation: it walks from the root, accumulating each width into an absolute offset and remembering the parent chain it passed through. Nothing about it is stored — ask again and it's rebuilt.

If @0
if @0
Call @3
Statements @12
absolute offsets + parent pointers, computed lazily
trivia
— anything in the source that's syntactically meaningless (doesn't change what the program does) but still has to round-trip for lossless text: whitespace, newlines, comments. Named to contrast with tokens (meaningful lexical units — keywords, identifiers, punctuation) and nodes (structural groupings of them, like If or Call). Prism's AST has tokens and nodes but zero trivia — it's exactly what this tree reconstructs from the gaps.

Format = rebuild trivia over the same nodes

Every Node-category element below stays exactly where it was — same kind, same order, same text. Only the Trivia leaves between them are discarded and resynthesized with a fixed rule (2-space indent per depth; blank-line runs of 2+ newlines in the original trivia collapse to exactly one). The rule only reads old trivia to decide the blank-line question — it never keeps the old spacing itself.

formatter_before.rbas written
canonical outputrebuilt trivia
    how the walk works — step through it →
    // This whole algorithm touches only the GREEN tree. No red tree is built,
// consulted, or needed — formatting never asks "where am I in the file?".
// depth isn't tree data either: it's a plain number threaded through the
// recursion, incremented by one each time the walk steps into a nested block.

fn format(node, depth) -> String:
    match node.kind:               // one arm per construct — see note below

        If | Unless:
            keyword   = node.token("if" or "unless")   // verbatim: "if"/"elsif"/"unless"
            predicate = format(node.first_child, depth)     // same depth — inline
            out = keyword + " " + predicate

            if node.has(Statements):
                // descending into the body — depth grows by exactly one
                out += "\n" + format_block(node.statements, depth + 1)

            if node.has(subsequent):     // another If (elsif) or an Else
                // same depth, no "end" here — the terminal clause owns it
                out += "\n" + indent(depth) + format(node.subsequent, depth)
            else:
                out += "\n" + indent(depth) + "end"

            return out

        // Else isn't its own arm above — stepping into one reuses these same two
        // regions (descend into body, then append "end"), since its shape is
        // identical: it's always the terminal clause.

        Call:
            return node.message + " " + format(node.arguments, depth)

        String:
            // a leaf: rendered verbatim from source, never rewritten —
            // only the trivia AROUND it is a formatting concern
            return source[node.start .. node.end]

        While | ClassNode | ArrayNode | ...:  // see note below
            ...


fn format_block(statements, depth) -> String:
    lines = []
    saw_blank = false
    for child in statements.children:   // still the GREEN tree — trivia included
        if child.category == Trivia:
            // read the OLD trivia just to answer one question,
            saw_blank = count("\n", child.text) >= 2
            continue                          // then discard its text entirely

        lines.push((saw_blank ? "\n" : "") + indent(depth) + format(child, depth))
        saw_blank = false

    return join(lines, "\n")
    formatter_before.rb
    The recursion mirrors the tree exactly, so the walk never needs to look sideways or backwards — each call only asks its own node "what are you, and what are your green-tree children?" No positions, no parent pointers, no red tree anywhere in this algorithm — depth is a local recursive accumulator, not something read off the tree. (Contrast with the Linter tab, which needs the red tree for exactly the parts this one doesn't.) See render / render_statements_block / render_conditional in src/bin/cst_playground.rs for the real version this is simplified from.
    The match node.kind above only has arms for what conditionals.rb exercises (If, Unless, Call, String, Arguments, Statements). A real formatter needs one arm per Ruby construct it can rewrite — conditionals (if/case), loops (while/until/for), collections (arrays, hashes), method calls and definitions, classes and modules, and so on — each with its own spacing rule, forever growing as coverage widens. tuxedo's own src/format/ has one file per construct family for exactly this reason (control_flow.rs, collections.rs, classes.rs, defs.rs, ...).

    A rule is a green-tree shape, reported at a red-tree position

    This reimplements the shape of RuboCop's Style/IfUnlessModifier: an If/Unless with exactly one statement and no elsif/else, short enough to fit on one line as a trailing modifier. The match only needs node kind and child count — portable, position-independent, green-tree work. Only the reported location and the stitched-together replacement text need the red tree's absolute offsets and source slices.

    conditionals.rb
    how a rule is evaluated — step through it →
    // A visitor: walk every node, test a shape at each one, recurse regardless
// of whether it matched (a violation can sit *inside* a non-violation).

fn check(node, diagnostics):

    if node.kind in (If, Unless):
        nodes = node.children.filter(category == Node)
        // pure green tree: kind + child count, nothing about position
        single_statement = nodes.len() == 2
            and nodes[1].kind == "Statements"
            and nodes[1].children_of_kind(Node).len() == 1

        if single_statement:
            // everything below needs the RED tree: "column" and "the actual text"
            // don't exist until you've walked from the root to get them
            line, col      = line_col(source, node.start)
            body_text      = source[body.start .. body.end]
            predicate_text = source[predicate.start .. predicate.end]
            replacement    = body_text + " " + keyword + " " + predicate_text

            if replacement.len() <= 80:
                diagnostics.push({ node.start, node.end, line, col, replacement })

    for child in node.children:    // every child, matched or not
        check(child, diagnostics)
    conditionals.rb
    The shape test and the recursion are pure green tree — portable, position-independent, and true regardless of where this code lives in a file or how many times it's copy-pasted. Only the highlighted middle block needs the red tree: converting a byte offset into a line/column, and slicing real source text by absolute range. Delete the red tree entirely and the rule still knows what to flag — it just can't say where, or produce the replacement text.
    the same rule, as a pattern instead of a walk
    // RuboCop ships exactly this: NodePattern, a small s-expression DSL that
// compiles down to the walking code above — you write the shape, not the walk.
// (illustrative syntax below, reconstructed from memory — not copy-pasted
// from RuboCop's source; treat the s-expression shape as the point, not
// the exact spelling.)

def_node_matcher :single_statement_modifier_candidate?, <<~PATTERN
  ({if unless} _condition [!begin? $_body] nil?)
PATTERN

// everything the pattern replaces:
if single_statement_modifier_candidate?(node):    // ← was the whole green-tree block above

    // everything the pattern does NOT replace — still hand-written, still red tree:
    line, col      = line_col(source, node.start)
    body_text      = source[body.start .. body.end]
    predicate_text = source[predicate.start .. predicate.end]
    replacement    = body_text + " " + keyword + " " + predicate_text

    if replacement.len() <= 80:
        diagnostics.push({ node.start, node.end, line, col, replacement })
    • {if unless} — alternation: matches either node kind
    • _condition — matches anything, unbound (a leading underscore is just a documentation name — no $, so nothing is captured)
    • [!begin? $_body] — two constraints on the same child: NOT a begin node (i.e. not multiple statements) AND capture it as body
    • nil? — the elsif/else slot must be empty
    The pattern only ever replaces the shape-matching half — the green-tree part. The moment the rule needs a position, a line/column, or the literal source text for a replacement, you're back in imperative code inside the match callback, exactly like the red-tree block above. RuboCop's NodePattern is one instance of a pattern; the same split shows up in tree-sitter's query language (a real, production green/red tree, same lineage as this playground) and in ESLint's CSS-like AST selectors (context.on("IfStatement > BlockStatement", fn)). None of them touch the red-tree half — they only save you from hand-walking nodes[1].children_of_kind(...).

    Semantic alignment: a column, checked against another column

    About the example: as first typed (no trailing \), Ruby treats each quoted line as its own statement — two orphan string literals with no effect (Lint/Void territory), not one continued append. Adding the line-continuation below is what actually makes prism merge the three literals into one InterpolatedString node spanning three lines — the semantic unit alignment cops check.

    RuboCop's layout/alignment cops don't compare trivia to a fixed rule the way the formatter does above — they compare one node's column to another node's column. That comparison is pure red tree: column only exists once you've walked from the root accumulating widths into an absolute offset, then found the last newline before it.

    alignment.rbas written
    correctedmoved to column
    how the rule is evaluated — step through it →
    // Same visitor shape as the Linter tab: walk everything, test a shape,
// recurse regardless. The difference is what the test compares.

fn check_alignment(node, diagnostics):

    if node.kind == "InterpolatedString":      // green tree: just a kind check
        parts = node.children_of_kind(Node)      // the concatenated String literals
        anchor, rest = parts[0], parts[1:]

        _, anchor_col = line_col(source, anchor.start)
        // ^ RED TREE: "column" doesn't exist until you walk from the root

        for part in rest:
            _, col = line_col(source, part.start)    // RED TREE again, per part
            if col != anchor_col:
                diagnostics.push({ part.start, part.end, anchor_col, col })

    for child in node.children:    // every child, matched or not
        check_alignment(child, diagnostics)
    alignment.rb
    The kind check and the recursion are green tree, exactly like the Linter tab. But here every single comparison is red-tree work — unlike Style/IfUnlessModifier, which only touched the red tree once to report a position, semantic alignment's entire job is comparing positions to each other. Take away the red tree and this rule has nothing left to check.

    The same file, parsed by a completely different tree

    This is a real, live tree-sitter-ruby parse running in your browser right now — not a simulation. The generic incremental engine (web-tree-sitter, the same C core every tree-sitter language shares, compiled to WASM) and the Ruby-specific grammar (tree-sitter-ruby, an independently authored package, also compiled to WASM) are both embedded directly in this page and run entirely client-side, with no server and no network fetch once the page has loaded.

    Every one of these ranges is plain whitespace that tree-sitter-ruby's grammar never turns into a token — comments become real extra nodes in this grammar, but spaces and most newlines don't. So this tree isn't lossless out of the box either: reconstructing exact source text from it needs the same trick as our own reconstruction earlier in this page — keep the original string, and treat any byte range no leaf node claims as trivia by elimination.
    Built by walking ruby_prism::Node locations (node spans + granular keyword/operator locations) and ParseResult::comments(), then filling every uncovered byte range with a reconstructed whitespace or comment leaf — see src/bin/cst_playground.rs. Node-kind support is scoped to what these four fixtures exercise (Program, Statements, If, Unless, Else, Call, Arguments, String, InterpolatedString).
